reason: The Qal perfect expresses the sufferer’s accusation of abandonment but cannot by itself prove an objective divine withdrawal or explain the cross.

rewrite.noticeThis: The cry names abandonment without euphemism, yet it remains prayer: “my God” is spoken twice. The verb tells us what the sufferer says to God; it does not by itself explain everything God is doing.
rewrite.whyItMatters: Scripture gives faithful suffering permission to accuse God of distance without severing the address. Yeshua takes Israel’s lament onto his own lips at the cross.

insight_issue: Lexical correction: עזב means forsake or leave, but its morphology does not adjudicate the theology or ontology of God’s action.

reason: The card coheres, but the insight wrongly derives complete and decisive withdrawal from the internal prefixes of ἐγκαταλείπω.
insight_issue: Lexical correction: ἐγκατέλιπες means “you forsook or abandoned me”; its contextual force should not be manufactured by separately theologizing its prefixes.

reason: The card faithfully distills Israel’s firstborn identity as God’s prior family claim against Pharaoh’s claim on their labor.
The insight says the exodus constitutes Israel as God’s son even though Exodus 4:22 names Israel as His son before the release.

rewrite.whyItMatters: God’s love and fatherly claim precede Israel’s rebellion. Hosea recalls the exodus so that Israel’s later betrayal—and God’s continuing compassion—can be felt as personal.

insight_issue: Contextual correction: the exodus displays and enacts God’s fatherly claim upon Israel rather than first creating that sonship.

reason: The card honors Hosea’s original reference to Israel while accurately presenting Matthew’s later typological application to Yeshua.
The card is sound, but the insight makes passive voice and כֹּל prove a definition and exceptionless scope that come instead from the passage’s stated inclusions.
insight_issue: Grammatical correction: Isaiah’s breadth rests on his explicit welcome of covenant-joining foreigners and eunuchs, not on the passive form or כֹּל alone.

reason: Both card and insight correctly see the den as refuge but overstate this by excluding wrongdoing within sacred space altogether.

rewrite.noticeThis: A den is a refuge robbers use, so Jeremiah accuses worshipers of treating the temple as cover after the crimes named in verses 9–10. The image emphasizes presumed safety, not a claim that no evil occurred within the sacred space.
rewrite.whyItMatters: God’s house cannot be used to make unrepented wrongdoing feel safe. The God whose name rests there also sees what worshipers hope respectability will conceal.

insight_issue: Interpretive correction: the den image emphasizes false refuge after wrongdoing but does not prove that no wrongdoing occurred at the temple.

reason: The prophetic combination is accurate, but the insight states the Court-of-the-Gentiles obstruction reconstruction more firmly than Mark permits.
insight_issue: Historical-inference correction: commerce obstructing the Gentile court is plausible but is not explicitly located or explained that way by Mark.

reason: The card faithfully preserves the appointed fish as both discipline and strange provision while adding a responsible safeguard about human captivity.
The card’s claim that the sign cannot be evaluated in advance goes beyond the insight and is too absolute because the comparison already announces a future event.

rewrite.noticeThis: Yeshua gives Jonah as the sign: as Jonah was enclosed for three days and nights, so the Son of Man will enter the heart of the earth. The comparison announces what lies ahead; the resurrection will disclose and vindicate its full meaning.

reason: The card faithfully distills the psalm’s exceptional ending in darkness and its permission for unresolved prayer.
The falling-word parallels consume space while the card overstates that the warning rests entirely on “living” rather than also on the judgment context of verse 30.

rewrite.noticeThis: The warning follows God’s declaration, “Vengeance is mine” (v.30). To fall into the living God’s hands is to face the Judge who acts—not an idea that can be dismissed.
rewrite.whyItMatters: This severe warning concerns deliberate turning from Christ, not ordinary doubt or a difficult season. Apostasy is not a private drift into nothingness but accountability before the living God.

reason: The card is coherent, but the insight incorrectly says direct command begins only in the final phrase when וְשַׁלַּח is already imperative.
insight_issue: Grammatical correction: the verse moves from infinitive absolutes into direct imperatives at “release the oppressed,” not only at the final verb.

reason: The card is appropriately cautious, but the insight falsely parses רֳאִי as a possessive form meaning “who sees me.”
insight_issue: Lexical correction: the local morphology identifies רֳאִי as an absolute noun without a first-person suffix, so “God who sees me” is contextual interpretation rather than transparent morphology.

reason: The card turns sincerity in calling into a warning against a preference-shaped doctrine of God, a defensible idea not developed by this insight.

rewrite.whyItMatters: God’s nearness is not earned by polished religious speech. He welcomes calling that is genuine—prayer in which our words and actual trust are not pulling in opposite directions.
rewrite.carryItWithYou: In your next prayer, leave out the polished version and tell God the real complaint, fear, or hope. Call on Him without pretending.

reason: The card fruitfully carries the study’s contextual recovery of “let go” or “stand down” without pretending the audience is certain.
The card faithfully limits “all things” to Paul’s changing circumstances and locates endurance in strength received from another.
Defining the good through verse 29 is contextually valuable but is an addition rather than a condensation of the supplied insight.

rewrite.noticeThis: The promise is bounded twice: it concerns those who love God, who are also called according to his purpose. It does not call every event good; it says the whole of life remains within God’s purposeful working.

reason: The card faithfully translates waiting as hopeful reliance and contrasts it with dependence on exhausted personal reserves.
The card retains the exile setting and improves application by refusing to appropriate Israel’s timetable or promised historical outcome.
The card faithfully condenses exhausting labor, externally laid weight, and rest personally supplied by Yeshua.
The card says the prayer was “answered, but not with removal,” while the insight calls it “the unanswered prayer.”
insight_issue: Narrative correction: the Lord answered Paul’s prayer with sufficient grace and power in weakness, although He did not grant the requested removal.

reason: The card preserves the physical support image while correctly distinguishing distrust of self-sufficient judgment from rejection of thought itself.
The card avoids the problem, but the insight wrongly makes the aorist require a single decisive release rather than a gradual or repeated practice.
insight_issue: Grammatical correction: the aorist participle links casting with humbling oneself but does not by itself prescribe an instantaneous psychological handoff.

reason: The card says the perfect does not settle perseverance, while the insight makes it prove that grace keeps believers saved from start to finish.
insight_issue: Grammatical correction: the construction presents a present saved condition resulting from God’s action but cannot alone settle every later question about perseverance.

reason: The card faithfully presents the cross as God’s continuing public demonstration of love toward people who were still sinners.
The card is cautious, but the insight too categorically dismisses “only begotten” and makes μονογενής decide a disputed theological question negatively.
insight_issue: Lexical correction: μονογενής securely marks the Son as unique, but the word alone should not be made to settle the eternal-generation question either way.

reason: The card accurately turns the psalm’s shift from “He” to “You” into a warm practice of direct address in suffering.
The card faithfully presents the chapter’s threefold command and grounds courage in God’s accompanying presence rather than temperament.
The card’s notice admits that the MT says “we are not consumed,” while its rendering and the insight make the first-person plural verb mean that God’s loyal loves never end.
insight_issue: Textual correction: the MT most naturally reads that the LORD’s loyal love is why “we are not consumed,” while “His loyal loves never cease” requires a labeled textual or interpretive adjustment.

reason: The card faithfully uses the emphatic negations as the author’s stated ground for freedom from money-love and anxious insecurity.
The card accurately limits the fear to punitive judgment and presents mature love as displacing dread of condemnation.
The card gives “things above” its immediate content in the enthroned Christ and carries that orientation into the chapter’s ordinary relationships.
The card faithfully connects Paul’s completed co-crucifixion with its present identity-shaping result and ongoing life of faith.
The card and insight call נִפְלֵיתִי and נִפְלָאִים the same root, but the local morphological corpus assigns them different lemmas.

rewrite.noticeThis: The psalmist’s own formation moves directly into praise of God’s wonderful works. The two Hebrew forms look related, but the local morphological text analyzes them as different lemmas, so the poetry should not be made to depend on an asserted repeated root.
rewrite.whyItMatters: This is not modern self-esteem detached from God. The psalmist receives his own embodied existence as a reason to stand in awe of the One whose works are wonderful.

insight_issue: Lexical correction: the local corpus tags נִפְלֵיתִי with Strong’s 6395 and נִפְלָאִים with 6381, so same-root repetition is not secure.

reason: The card faithfully retains the promise of covenant presence through danger while refusing to turn it into universal physical immunity.
